items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we will explore strategies for parametrizing cylinders.

Content:
Parametrizing a cylinder is no more difficult than parametrizing its base curve. The only difference is that we need a second parameter to control the variation parallel to the cylinder's axis. This second parameter is usually allowed to vary arbitrarily.

Content:
For example, consider the parabolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as

Content:
[MATH: y = 8x^2.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: y = y(x)] is an explicit function of [MATH: x.] Therefore, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on this surface, we have

Content:
[MATH: f(x, z)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨x, 8x^{2}, z⟩.]

Content:
And that's it! We have successfully found a parametrization of this cylinder.

Content:
Note that, under this parametrization

Content:
- the parameter [MATH: x \in (-\infty,\infty)] controls the movement along the base curve, and
- the parameter [MATH: z \in (-\infty,\infty)] controls the movement parallel to the [MATH: z]-axis.

Content:
Let's see some more examples.

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{z^2}{16}=1.]

Content:
The base curve in the [MATH: xz]-plane is an ellipse centered at [MATH: O] with semi-axes of lengths [MATH: \sqrt{25} = 5] and [MATH: \sqrt{16} = 4.] Therefore, we can parametrize the base curve in the [MATH: xz]-plane as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \langle x,z \rangle = \big\langle 5\cos{t}, \: 4\sin{t} \big\rangle,

where [MATH: t \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: y \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Content:
Note that the axis of the cylinder coincides with the [MATH: y]-axis. Therefore, the parameter [MATH: y] is allowed to vary arbitrarily.

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(t,z)] above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1.] What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(t,z) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: 4\sin{t}, \: z \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(t,z)] above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1.] What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the ellipse [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1] in [MATH: xy]-plane has the parametrization [MATH: \langle x,y \rangle = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 4\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi),]

since

[MATH: (x^{2})/(4) + (y^{2})/(16)|= ((2\cos t)^{2})/(4) + ((4\sin t)^{2})/(16); = (4\cos^{2} t)/(4) + (16\sin^{2} t)/(16); = \cos^{2} t + \sin^{2} t; = 1.]

Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

[MATH: f(t, z)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨2\cos t, 4\sin t, z⟩]

where [MATH: t \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: z \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Therefore, the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{blue}2\cos{t}}.]

where [MATH: t \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] and [MATH: y \in (-\infty, \infty).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will explore strategies for parametrizing cylinders.

Content:
Parametrizing a cylinder is no more difficult than parametrizing its base curve. The only difference is that we need a second parameter to control the variation parallel to the cylinder's axis. This second parameter is usually allowed to vary arbitrarily.

Content:
For example, consider the parabolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as

Content:
[MATH: y = 8x^2.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: y = y(x)] is an explicit function of [MATH: x.] Therefore, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on this surface, we have

Content:
[MATH: f(x, z)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨x, 8x^{2}, z⟩.]

Content:
And that's it! We have successfully found a parametrization of this cylinder.

Content:
Note that, under this parametrization

Content:
- the parameter [MATH: x \in (-\infty,\infty)] controls the movement along the base curve, and
- the parameter [MATH: z \in (-\infty,\infty)] controls the movement parallel to the [MATH: z]-axis.

Content:
Let's see some more examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Parametrizing a Parabolic Cylinder

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(x,y) = \big\langle x, \: y, \: \text{___} \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(x,y)] above parametrizes the parabolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: 2x^2=z.] What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

[MATH: f(x, y)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨x, y, 2x^{2}⟩]

where [MATH: x \in (-\infty,\infty)] and [MATH: y \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Therefore, the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{blue} 2x^2}.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Elliptic Cylinders

Content:
Let's find a parametrization of the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{z^2}{16}=1.]

Content:
The base curve in the [MATH: xz]-plane is an ellipse centered at [MATH: O] with semi-axes of lengths [MATH: \sqrt{25} = 5] and [MATH: \sqrt{16} = 4.] Therefore, we can parametrize the base curve in the [MATH: xz]-plane as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \langle x,z \rangle = \big\langle 5\cos{t}, \: 4\sin{t} \big\rangle,
\qquad t \in [0,2\pi).]

Content:
Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following parametrization:

Content:
[MATH: f(t, y)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨5\cos t, y, 4\sin t⟩]

Content:
where [MATH: t \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: y \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Content:
Note that the axis of the cylinder coincides with the [MATH: y]-axis. Therefore, the parameter [MATH: y] is allowed to vary arbitrarily.

---

Item 6 — Example: Parametrizing an Elliptic Cylinder

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(t,z) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: 4\sin{t}, \: z \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(t,z)] above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1.] What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the ellipse [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1] in [MATH: xy]-plane has the parametrization
[MATH: \langle x,y \rangle = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 4\sin{t} \big\rangle,
\qquad t \in [0,2\pi),]

since

[MATH: (x^{2})/(4) + (y^{2})/(16)|= ((2\cos t)^{2})/(4) + ((4\sin t)^{2})/(16); = (4\cos^{2} t)/(4) + (16\sin^{2} t)/(16); = \cos^{2} t + \sin^{2} t; = 1.]

Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

[MATH: f(t, z)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨2\cos t, 4\sin t, z⟩]

where [MATH: t \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: z \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Therefore, the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{blue}2\cos{t}}.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Hyperbolic Cylinders

Content:
To find a parametrization of one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{25}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1]

Content:
for [MATH: x \geq 5,] recall that the corresponding hyperbola in [MATH: xy]-plane has the parametrization

Content:
[MATH: \langle x,y \rangle = \big\langle 5 \sec{t}, \: 4 \tan{t} \big\rangle,
\qquad t\in\left(-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right)]

Content:
We can check that this indeed parametrizes our base hyperbola by substituting the parametric equations into the equation of the base curve:

Content:
[MATH: (x^{2})/(25) − (y^{2})/(16)|= ((5\sec t)^{2})/(25) − ((4\tan t)^{2})/(16); = \sec^{2} t − \tan^{2} t; = 1]

Content:
Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: f(t, z)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨5\sec t, 4\tan t, z⟩]

Content:
where [MATH: t\in\left(-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right)] and [MATH: z \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Item 10 — Example: Parametrizing a Hyperbolic Cylinder

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(t,y)] above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: \dfrac{z^2}{4} - \dfrac{x^2}{16} = 1] for [MATH: z \geq 2.] What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the hyperbola [MATH: \dfrac{z^2}{4} - \dfrac{x^2}{16} = 1] for [MATH: z \geq 2] in [MATH: xz]-plane has the parametrization
[MATH: \langle x , z \rangle = \big \langle 4\tan{t}, \, 2\sec{t} \big\rangle,

\qquad t \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)]

since
[MATH: (z^{2})/(4) − (x^{2})/(16)|= ((2\sec t)^{2})/(4) − ((4\tan t)^{2})/(16); = (4\sec^{2} t)/(4) − (16\tan^{2} t)/(16); = \sec^{2} t − \tan^{2} t; = 1.]

Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:
[MATH: f(t, y)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨4\tan t, y, 2\sec t⟩]

where [MATH: t \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)] and [MATH: y \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Therefore, the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{blue}2\sec{t}}.]
